title: Weather station: wind and rain sensors, reed switches and magnets
summary: A home weather station has a sensor array outdoors (wind cups and vane, a tipping rain bucket, a temperature and humidity sensor) and a console indoors with a barometer and display. Take the sensors and their reed switches and magnets in about 20 minutes. The main danger is falling from a roof or ladder, and touching a power line with a metal mast.

steps.text: Start with the console indoors. Put in fresh batteries or plug it in. If it shows the time, indoor temperature and air pressure, keep it whole: it is a working barometer, and its pressure trend is the most useful thing in the kit. Only strip it for parts if it is dead.
Find the outdoor array. It is usually on a pole, fence post, balcony rail or roof bracket, and may be a cable or wireless unit. Look up and around the mount first, then decide how you will reach it.
steps.warn: Check for overhead power lines before you lift a metal pole or ladder. A mast that touches a line can kill you. If you can't reach it from the ground or a firm ladder, leave it.

steps.text: Stand a ladder on firm, level ground with a helper footing it. Take the batteries out of the array (usually AA or a lithium coin or CR123 cell, under a small cover) so nothing is live while you work.
steps.warn: Don't carry tools in your hands on a ladder. Keep three points of contact and don't overreach.

steps.text: Undo the mounting clamp (2–4 nuts on a U-bolt or a single wing nut) and bring the whole array down to the ground. For a wired unit, unplug or cut the cable at the console end and keep its length with the plug.

Anemometer: pull the wind cups off their hub, or unscrew the central screw. A small magnet sits in the rotor. A reed switch or Hall sensor on the circuit board below gives one pulse per turn. Keep the cups and the shaft with its tiny bearings.
Wind vane: take off the arrow. A magnet (or several) sits in the vane base over reed switches, or a small variable resistor reads direction. Keep the vane, its shaft and its bearings together.

Rain gauge: lift out the funnel (clips or 2 screws) and the tipping bucket, a small seesaw that tips each time it fills. A small magnet on the bucket passes a reed switch, which clicks once for each tip. Keep the bucket and its switch together if you may rebuild a gauge.
Unclip the white louvred plates that shade the temperature and humidity sensor. Take out the small sensor board by its edges. Don't touch the sensor chip with your fingers.
steps.warn: Reed switches are small glass tubes. They snap if you bend their wire legs close to the glass.

steps.text: If the top has a small solar cell, unscrew it with its leads. If the array has a small circuit board with the radio transmitter, take it whole, with its antenna wire. Don't cut the board; the radio parts are tiny.

Test the switches. Set the meter to continuity (see test_continuity) and probe the two wires of each reed switch while you pass a magnet near it: it should beep when the magnet is close. A good wind or rain sensor closes once for each turn or tip.
Bag small parts by type (magnets with magnets, switches with switches). Keep the small magnets away from compasses, cards and electronics, or they will upset them.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Console and barometer.** Keep it working if you can. A steady fall of air pressure (about 6 hPa or more in three hours) usually means a storm is coming; a steady rise means settling weather. Even a rough record in a notebook is useful for farming, sailing and planning trips.
- **Reed switches and magnets.** Glass-sealed switches that close when a magnet comes close. Use them as door or window alarm sensors, bicycle speedometer sensors, flow-meter counters and rev counters (see build_perimeter_alarm).
- **Wind cups and sensor.** A cup anemometer typically gives about 3–4 km/h of wind speed for each turn per second. Calibrate it by holding it out of a car window on a calm day at a known speed. Use it to find a good site for a wind turbine before you build one.
- **Rain gauge bucket.** Each tip is a fixed amount of rain, often 0.2 mm or 0.01 inch. Calibrate by pouring a measured cup of water through the funnel and counting the tips.
- **Temperature and humidity board.** A small sensor that works with an Arduino-style board; the humidity element is delicate.
- **Small bearings.** Tiny ball bearings from the cups and vane.
- **Solar cell.** A small 3–5 V cell that charges a small cell or runs a little light.
- **433 or 915 MHz radio parts.** A sensor transmitter and receiver. Handy for a wireless alarm or sensor project, but not easy to repurpose.

## Variations

- Wired stations (like some Davis models) send readings along a thin four-wire cable. The cable is a useful length of low-voltage wire.
- Newer all-in-one arrays use an ultrasonic wind sensor with no moving parts, so no cups, vane or reed switch.
- Cheap garden thermometers and wireless thermometers hold little more than a temperature sensor and a display.
- Farm, marina and school stations are sometimes bigger, with a data logger and a small solar panel or battery (see safety_lead_acid if one has a lead-acid battery).

## What to leave

- The plastic housings and mounting poles, unless you need the pole.
- The display glass of the console once it is dead.
